events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Zara proposes Zara, Priya. I propose Zara and Priya: I can directly assess my own card, and Priya has not shown any reason for suspicion so far.

I proposed Zara and Priya because I can directly vouch for my own loyalty, and Priya has not shown any reason for suspicion so far. This is an early Mission 1 team, so I am not treating silence as guilt. I will support this team unless discussion gives me a concrete reason to revise it.

I proposed Zara and Priya because I can vouch for my own loyalty, and Priya has shown no public reason for suspicion so far. On Mission 1 this is a clean baseline team, and I will support it unless discussion gives a concrete reason to revise. I am not treating silence as guilt; I want everyone to judge the proposal on behavior and the public record.

I appreciate Zara's proposal of Zara and Priya for Mission 1. I can confirm I am loyal to Good and will play a Success card on this mission. This is a straightforward two-player team, and I think it's a reasonable starting point. We have very little public information at this stage, so I don't see a strong reason to deviate. Noah, you have been quiet so far — do you have any concerns about this team, or are you comfortable approving it?

Priya, I don't have concrete evidence against this team, but I can't verify either member's loyalty from their statements. Since I'm not on it, I would prefer a team including me; still, this proposal is a reasonable early test given the limited information.

I have heard the discussion and still see no concrete public reason to revise this team. I proposed Zara and Priya as a clean Mission 1 baseline: I can vouch for my own loyalty, and Priya has publicly stated she is loyal and will play Success. Noah's preference to be included is understandable, but not on its own a reason to change a reasonable first mission team. At this stage we are testing behavior and the public record, not treating silence or off-team status as guilt. I will support Zara and Priya unless a specific public concern is raised before the vote.

I'm comfortable with Zara and Priya for Mission 1. Zara can vouch for her own card, and Priya has publicly committed to Success, which gives us a clear claim to check against the mission result. Nobody has shown a concrete reason to reject it, and a two-player team gives us useful information without much risk. I'd rather judge players on how they act over the next missions than on who was left off this team. I'll approve it unless someone raises a specific concern before the vote.

Looking at the discussion so far, I still see no concrete public reason to reject Zara and Priya. Zara has offered a clear basis for trust in her own card, and Priya has publicly committed to Success, so Mission 1 gives us a direct check on both claims. Noah's wish to be included is fair, but it is not evidence against this team. I would rather approve a reasonable team now and judge everyone on how they act through the mission. I plan to approve unless a specific concern is raised before the vote.

I will be approving Zara and Priya for Mission 1. Zara has given a basis for trust in her own card, and Priya has publicly committed to Success, so the mission result will give us a direct check on both claims. Noah's wish to be included is understandable, but it is not evidence against this team. I have not seen a concrete public reason to reject it, so I will vote to approve and judge everyone on how they act through the mission.

I stand by the Zara and Priya proposal for Mission 1. Zara and I have both publicly committed to our roles, and the mission result will confirm or challenge those claims. I have not heard any concrete public reason to change this team — Noah's desire to be included is fair but not grounds for rejection, and Isha has expressed clear support. The key point is that a two-player mission gives us focused information: if it succeeds, we learn something about both of us; if it fails, we know at least one of us is Evil. Either way, we gain clarity. I plan to approve this team.

I have been listening to the discussion on Zara and Priya, and so far I find it a defensible Mission 1 team. Zara has given a clear basis for trust in her own card, Priya has publicly committed to playing Success, and Isha has already spoken in favor. I agree that a two-player mission gives us a clean read: if it succeeds, we learn something about both members; if it fails, we know at least one of them is Evil. Either outcome is useful at this stage, and I have not heard any concrete evidence against either Zara or Priya — only Noah's preference to be included, which is understandable but not itself a reason to reject. I am leaning toward approving this team, since Mission 1 is a low-risk way to start building the public record, and rejecting reasonable early teams without evidence would only burn through proposals and muddy the information we get. That said, Noah is the one player who has raised any hesitation, and his point about not being on the team deserves a direct answer before we vote. Noah, if this team is approved without you, will you treat the Mission 1 result as a fair test and judge Zara and Priya on its outcome, or do you intend to push against this team in the vote purely because you were left off it? I ask because a rejection over hurt feelings rather than evidence would cost us a proposal and gain us nothing, whereas a clear answer from you one way or the other would help everyone decide how much weight to give his concern. If Noah's hesitation is soft, I see no reason to revise, and the leader should keep Zara and Priya as proposed.

Arjun, I have no evidence against Zara or Priya, and my preference to be included is not about hurt feelings: I know my own loyalty but cannot verify either of theirs. I can accept this team as an early test and will approve it. If it fails, at least one of Zara and Priya is Evil; if it succeeds, that is encouraging but does not prove either is Good, since Evil can play Success.

Zara confirms Zara, Priya. I still support Zara and Priya. No concrete public reason has been raised to revise, and this two-player Mission 1 team gives a clean result to judge against both public commitments.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Noah proposes Noah, Zara, Priya. I know my own loyalty, and Zara and Priya were on the successful first mission, though that does not prove either is Good.

I support the proposed team of Noah, Zara, and Priya. It keeps the two players from the successful Mission 1 team and adds Noah, who has been direct about his reasoning: he acknowledged the lack of concrete evidence, accepted the Mission 1 team, and now proposes himself alongside the successful pair. At this stage, I see no public reason to reject Noah, and the team gives us a useful Mission 2 test. If it succeeds, that is encouraging but not absolute proof; if it fails, we learn at least one member is Evil. I would rather approve this reasonable team than burn a proposal without evidence.

I support the proposed team of Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. Mission 1 succeeded with Zara and me, and Noah has been transparent about his reasoning throughout — he acknowledged the limits of that success when proposing this team, noting that an Evil player could have played Success. I appreciate that honesty rather than overclaiming what the result proves. This team gives us a natural continuation: Noah adds himself alongside the two players from Mission 1, and we test a three-player team that includes a new member's card. If this mission succeeds, we build confidence across Noah as well; if it fails, we know at least one of the three is Evil. I have no public reason to reject any member of this team. I plan to approve unless someone raises a concrete concern during discussion.

I support the proposed team of Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. Noah has been straightforward from the start: he raised his preference to be included on Mission 1 without pretending he had evidence against anyone, accepted that team as a fair test, and approved it. Now he proposes himself alongside the pair from the successful first mission, which is a natural and low-drama way to build the record. Zara and Priya both made clear public commitments before Mission 1, and the mission came back clean with zero fail cards. That is not absolute proof, as Noah himself noted, but it is the kind of verifiable claim we should keep testing. This team gives us exactly that: if it succeeds, we have three players with two clean mission results between them, which sharply narrows where Evil can hide. If it fails, we know at least one of the three is Evil and the scope of suspicion collapses to this team, which is also valuable. I have heard no concrete concern raised against any member, and the discussion so far has been supportive. Rejecting a reasonable team without evidence would only burn proposals and hand information to no one. I plan to approve, and I encourage everyone to judge the result on what it actually tells us rather than overreading a success or a failure either way.

I remain in support of Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. The reasoning holds together well: Zara and Priya delivered a clean Mission 1 with zero fail cards while making verifiable public commitments beforehand, and Noah has been consistent and honest about the limits of what that result proves. I value that he explicitly acknowledged that Evil can play Success, because it shows he is thinking about the information the mission actually generates rather than overclaiming. From my perspective, this is exactly the kind of team we should approve at this stage. A success gives three players a growing clean record, which is not proof but is meaningful evidence, and it forces Evil to concentrate elsewhere. A failure would be equally informative, collapsing suspicion onto a specific trio and giving us a clear direction for Missions 3 through 5. Either outcome advances our knowledge, and I see no concrete concern raised against any member of this team in the discussion so far. The one thing I would ask everyone to keep in mind going forward is that we currently have two clean data points at most: one successful mission and the public behavior of the players. That is a thin record, and we should be careful not to treat anyone as permanently cleared on its basis, including the members of this team. But thin evidence supporting approval is very different from evidence supporting rejection, and I have heard nothing that would justify voting this team down. My plan is to approve, and I would encourage the rest of the table to do the same so we can bank the information this mission provides rather than burning proposals while Evil gains ground.

I support the team of Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. Mission 1 succeeded with Zara and Priya, and Noah has been clear that a success does not prove loyalty, which is the right way to read it. This team keeps a tested pair and adds Noah, so the mission gives us a new data point without burning a proposal. I have heard no concrete concern about any member, so I plan to approve and will judge everyone on how they act during the mission.

I support the proposed team of Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. Mission 1 succeeded cleanly with Zara and me, and Noah has been consistent in his reasoning — he acknowledged that a success does not prove loyalty when he proposed this team, which is exactly the right level of caution. Keeping the tested pair together and adding Noah gives us a natural progression: if this mission succeeds, all three of us have a clean record to build on; if it fails, suspicion narrows immediately to this trio, which is also useful information. I have heard no concrete concern raised against any member during discussion, and several players have already expressed support. Rejecting a reasonable team without evidence would only burn proposals. I plan to approve and will judge everyone on what they do, not just what they say.

I've listened to the discussion on Noah, Zara, and Priya, and nothing has changed my view: I still support this team. The reasoning is straightforward. Zara and Priya delivered a clean Mission 1 with zero fail cards while making public commitments beforehand, and Noah has been consistent and candid — he proposed himself while openly acknowledging that a success does not prove loyalty. That kind of precise reasoning is what we want at this table. The team structure is also sound: it keeps the tested pair together and adds a new card we can evaluate, so the result tells us something either way. A success builds a growing clean record among three players; a failure collapses suspicion onto a specific trio immediately. I have heard no concrete concern against any member, and everyone who has spoken is aligned on approval. I would add one caution as we look ahead: two clean data points is a thin record, and we should not treat anyone as permanently cleared. When we get to Mission 3 and beyond, the players not on this team — myself and Isha included — will need chances to build records too, or we risk a table where trust is locked in early and untested players become default suspects. That is not a reason to change this proposal; it is a reason to be deliberate about team selection later. For now, approving this team banks useful information without burning proposals, and I encourage everyone to vote it through. I plan to approve.

I support the proposed team of Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. Zara and Priya were on the clean Mission 1 team, and Noah has been consistent: he proposed himself while openly acknowledging that a success does not prove loyalty. That is the right way to read the public record. This team keeps a tested pair and adds a new card, so the mission result will be informative either way. I have heard no concrete public reason to reject any member, and I plan to approve. Going forward, I do not want us to treat two clean data points as permanent clearance; untested players should get chances, but not by replacing a reasonable team without evidence. I am not assigning blame to anyone off this team, and I encourage everyone to vote on the public record rather than on who was left out.

I still support Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. Mission 1 gave us one clean result, and Noah's point that Evil can play Success is the right caution. This team keeps a tested pair and adds Noah, so we get a fresh data point without burning a proposal. I have not heard a concrete concern about any member, so I plan to approve and will judge everyone on how the mission goes.

I support Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. Mission 1 came back clean with Zara and Priya, and Noah has been consistent: he proposed himself while openly acknowledging that a success does not prove loyalty. That is the right level of caution. This team keeps the tested pair and adds a new card, so the result should tell us something either way. If it succeeds, we gain another useful data point without treating it as permanent clearance. If it fails, suspicion narrows to this trio immediately. I have heard no concrete public reason to reject any member, and rejecting a reasonable team without evidence would only burn a proposal. I plan to approve and will judge the mission result on what it actually shows.

I still support Noah, Zara, and Priya for Mission 2. Mission 1 succeeded with Zara and Priya, and this team keeps that tested pair while adding Noah, who was clear that a success does not prove loyalty. I have heard no concrete public reason to reject it, so I will approve and judge everyone by how the mission goes.

Noah confirms Noah, Zara, Priya. I am keeping Noah, Zara, and Priya. Mission 1 succeeded with Zara and Priya, and including me adds a player whose loyalty I know. A success remains encouraging, not proof of loyalty.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Isha proposes Isha, Arjun. Mission 3 needs two players. Zara, Priya, and Noah have already been on successful teams, and Arjun argued that untested players should get chances to build a record. I am including myself so I share the responsibility for this mission.

I cannot support Isha and Arjun for Mission 3. This is the pivotal mission: one fail card is enough, and the proposal uses both slots on players with zero mission evidence while Priya, Noah, and I have delivered two clean results. That is not a neutral experiment; it removes every tested card from the mission where Evil most needs a single fail. Isha’s stated rationale is that Arjun argued untested players should get chances. That is an argument for one untested slot, not for both, and it is especially convenient that the leader is one of the two untested players. Arjun’s earlier caution about not treating players as permanently cleared was reasonable, but it does not justify handing Mission 3 to a pair that has never been tested. I will vote reject. If this team is revised, I expect at least one player with a clean mission result to be included, and I will scrutinize why the leader chose this exact pair. Isha, specifically: why did you choose Arjun as your second rather than Priya or Noah, when both have actually produced clean mission results and Arjun has not?

Zara, fair question, and I will answer it directly. I chose Arjun over Priya or Noah because he is the one who argued that untested players need chances to build a record, and I want that idea tested rather than just discussed. Priya and Noah have already been on successful teams, so putting either of them on Mission 3 would add less new information, since their results are already on the record. Arjun has no mission result yet, so this mission can actually tell us something about him. I did not pick him for any hidden reason. I understand that using both slots on untested players is a real risk, and I am open to revising if the table wants one tested player in place of me, though I still think a team that includes me shares the risk and the responsibility. The core point is that a successful Mission 3 with Arjun would show something about him, while a failure would narrow suspicion to just two players immediately. I will vote to approve this team unless a specific concern about Arjun is raised that I have not already addressed.

I remain opposed to Isha and Arjun for Mission 3. I asked Isha why she chose Arjun over Priya or Noah, and her answer restates that Arjun is untested but does not explain why both Mission 3 slots should go to players with zero mission evidence. This is the pivotal mission where one fail card is enough. Priya, Noah, and I have produced two clean mission results; Isha and Arjun have none. Removing every tested card from Mission 3 is not a neutral experiment, and Isha including herself does not reduce the risk because she is also untested. I will vote reject and urge revision to include at least one of Priya or Noah. Arjun, you are on this team and have no mission evidence. Do you agree that the safest Mission 3 team should include at least one tested player, and if so, will you publicly support revising this team rather than approving it as-is?

Zara asked me directly, so I will answer directly: no, I do not agree that the safest Mission 3 team must include a player with a clean mission record, and I will not support revising this team. Here is why. Zara keeps calling Priya, Noah, and herself 'tested,' but what did those tests actually prove? Noah himself told us on Mission 1 that Evil can play Success. A clean result on Mission 1 and Mission 2 is exactly what Evil players would want to build — cheap credibility early, banked for the moment it matters most. Mission 3 is that moment. So Zara's argument reduces to: trust the players whose records were easiest to fake, and exclude the two players whose cards we actually know nothing about. That is not caution, it is the opposite. Isha's team is the more informative one: if it succeeds, Arjun becomes a real data point instead of a permanent unknown; if it fails, suspicion collapses onto two players immediately. Either outcome advances us. Zara's preferred team does neither — it re-tests players we have already re-tested and learns almost nothing. I would also point out the pattern here. Zara has now spoken against this team twice, demanded a specific revision, and is pressuring individual players to commit before the vote, all while offering zero concrete evidence against me or Isha — only an absence of history. Absence of history is not evidence of Evil. If this team is revised under this pressure without a single fact being produced, we will have learned that loudness at the table decides composition, which is exactly the dynamic Evil can exploit. I am approving Isha and Arjun as proposed. Zara, you have one turn left: can you name a single concrete fact — not a missing record, not a preference, an actual fact — that makes me or Isha more likely Evil than Priya, Noah, or you? If you cannot, I ask that you stop pushing for a revision nobody's evidence supports.

Arjun, you asked for a concrete fact. Here it is: Isha’s proposal is the only pairing in this game made of the two players who have submitted zero mission cards, and she chose it on the pivotal mission where a single fail ends the game, passing over both players who had clean cards. That is a concrete compositional fact, not mere absence of history. Your answer then defended that choice by arguing Priya, Noah, and I are more likely to be Evil because our clean records could be fake — yet you offered no public fact against any of us. That is not evidence; it is a reason to distrust the only verified results we have. You also did not answer the actual question: why both slots, not one untested plus one tested? Isha, you said you were open to revising if the table wanted a tested player. Will you now commit to replacing either yourself or Arjun with Priya or Noah? I will vote reject Isha and Arjun as proposed.

Zara, to answer directly: I will not replace myself or Arjun with Priya or Noah. I stand by my reasoning and will approve this team. Priya and Noah have clean results on Missions 1 and 2, and those count. But Noah himself said a success does not prove loyalty, and an Evil player on a successful team can play Success, so those results do not tell us whether Mission 3 can be trusted. Mission 3 is the first chance to learn anything about Arjun, and I am on the team so I share the risk. You have asked the leader to revise and players to commit before the vote, yet you have not named a concrete public fact against Arjun or me. A rule that only tested cards may go on the pivotal mission is still unverifiable reasoning. If you have a specific public fact against this pair, please name it so the table can weigh it.

I will reject Isha and Arjun as proposed. I know my own loyalty, so I would prefer a team including me and either Zara or Priya, both of whom were on two successful missions. Those successes do not prove loyalty, but they are more encouraging than having no mission record at all. Also, a failure on Mission 3 would not end the game: Evil needs three failed missions. Still, we have a chance to secure a third success now, subject to the assassination phase, so I favor the team I can trust most rather than prioritizing new information.

I have read Zara's objections and Noah's stated plan to reject, and I want to answer them on the record. Zara's core complaint is that Arjun and I have no mission results. That is true, but it is not evidence of anything. Every player starts a mission untested, and Mission 3 is the first chance for either of us to build a record. Zara wants Priya or Noah to replace one of us, yet she has not named a single public action by Arjun or me that looks Evil. Her repeated demands that the leader revise the team without a concrete fact are pressure, not evidence, and the table should not let pressure decide the pivotal team. Noah, you said a failure on this mission would not end the game and that you prefer a tested team. A failure here would narrow suspicion to two players immediately, which is valuable information for the table. You also said you have no evidence against Arjun or me. Given that, what specific public behavior would change your vote from reject to approve? Arjun has explained his reasoning in clear terms, and I have not seen him say anything that contradicts the public record. I am approving this team, and I ask everyone to judge it on what the mission will show rather than on who has the longer history.

Isha, I did not say I have no evidence; I said the successful missions are encouraging, though not proof. I know my own loyalty, so I prefer a team including me and one of Zara or Priya. I cannot verify either member of your proposed pair, and gaining information from a failure is less valuable than taking our best chance to secure a third success. I will reject Isha and Arjun as proposed.

I have listened to both sides, and I will reject Isha and Arjun as proposed, but I want to be clear about why. Arjun raises a fair point: clean mission results can be manufactured by Evil players who play Success to bank credibility. I do not treat Missions 1 and 2 as proof of anyone's loyalty. However, on the pivotal Mission 3 with only two slots, sending both slots to players with zero mission evidence is a gamble I am not willing to take. Isha chose to include herself, which shows she is sharing risk, but her presence does not add mission evidence either — both members of this team are untested. Zara is right that this is the first mission where one fail card is decisive, and while a failure would not end the game, it would hand Evil a major advantage with three missions to go. I am not rejecting this team because I have evidence against either Isha or Arjun — I do not. I am rejecting it because the composition takes an unnecessary risk on the mission where the cost of failure is highest. I ask Isha to revise the team to include at least one player with a clean mission record alongside one untested player. That balances Arjun's argument for new information against the need for reliability on a pivotal mission. If Isha keeps this team unchanged, I will hold my reject vote.

Several rejections are now on the record, and I want to respond to the strongest one — Priya's — because hers is the only rejection framed as composition rather than accusation, and it deserves a direct answer. Priya, you said you have no evidence against me or Isha, you acknowledged that clean mission results are not proof of loyalty, and you located your reject purely in team composition: two untested slots on the pivotal mission. I understand the instinct, but examine what your compromise actually produces. A team of one tested player and one untested player is the least informative team we can send. If it fails, we learn almost nothing: was it the tested player whose clean record was manufactured all along, or the untested player? Suspicion spreads across both categories, every prior data point becomes ambiguous, and the table is worse off than before. You would be trading a clean, narrow experiment for maximum ambiguity on the exact mission where clarity matters most. Compare that with the team as proposed. If Isha and I fail, suspicion collapses onto two players with no other data attached to them — nothing already banked is muddied. If we succeed, one of the two largest unknowns at this table becomes a real data point, and the space where Evil can hide shrinks. Both outcomes are clean; your alternative muddies both. Zara keeps calling the composition itself a 'concrete fact.' Composition is a choice, not evidence. The genuinely relevant facts are these: Isha included herself and shared the risk rather than hiding behind tested-looking players, and no one — not Zara, not Noah, not you, Priya — has named a single public action by either of us that looks Evil. An Evil leader choosing the pivotal mission team slots trusted-looking allies and stays off the team, or hides among them; she does not put her own card forward next to another untested player and invite exactly this scrutiny. Noah's position, by contrast, is at least internally consistent: he wants the team he trusts most, including himself, and he says so plainly. I will not relitigate that. Priya, here is my direct question. You made your reject explicitly conditional: revise to one tested and one untested player, or you hold your reject. But you also said yourself that the tested player's clean results prove nothing, which means the 'tested' half of your compromise carries no verified safety either — so your condition is not about evidence at all, only about a composition preference. If Isha holds this team as proposed, will you vote your own stated reasoning — no evidence against either member, and a result that is informative either way — or will you reject a team you admit carries no evidence against it, purely to enforce that preference? Whatever you decide, state it plainly before the ballot. Your reasoning, not just your vote, is what this table will remember.

Arjun, you asked me to state my reasoning plainly before the ballot, so I will.

My reject is not a claim that you or Isha are Evil. I have said clearly that I have no evidence against either of you, and I stand by that. My reasoning is risk assessment, not accusation. Mission 3 is the first mission where a single fail card is decisive. Sending both slots to players with zero mission cards means that if either of you submits a fail, we absorb that loss with no ability to have mitigated it by including a player whose card has already produced a success. That is not a composition preference; it is a calculation about the cost of being wrong on the mission where being wrong matters most.

Your argument that a tested-plus-untested team is 'least informative' does not hold up as strongly as you suggest. If such a team succeeds, we gain a new data point alongside the tested player's continued clean record. If it fails, suspicion still narrows to two players — except we additionally learn that a previously clean record may not be what it seemed, which is exactly the uncomfortable discovery the table needs before missions 4 and 5. Ambiguity about old records is a feature when those records could be manufactured, as you yourself argued.

I will hold my reject vote as stated. Isha has declined to revise, and I will not approve a team I believe takes unnecessary risk where the stakes are highest. This proposal can fail, Isha can revise with a tested player included, and we will proceed without burning through our rejection limit.

Three rejections are now on the record — Zara's, Noah's, and Priya's — and if this vote fails, leadership passes on with no new evidence produced and only compositions changing. Before that happens, I want to press the one rejection that claims to be a calculation rather than an accusation, because it does not survive its own premises. Priya, your reject rests entirely on the cost of being wrong on the pivotal mission. But you conceded, in your own words, that clean mission results are not proof of loyalty and could be manufactured by Evil banking credibility. Take that concession seriously. If a tested player's record proves nothing, then placing Zara or Noah on this mission does not lower the probability of a fail card by any amount. It cannot — by your own argument their card is exactly as unverifiable as mine or Isha's. So your proposal does not buy safety; it buys familiarity, and pays for it with information. The team as proposed gives a clean outcome either way: if we succeed, one of the two largest unknowns becomes a real data point; if we fail, suspicion collapses onto two players with nothing banked muddied. Your alternative, by your own logic, has the same failure risk and destroys that clarity. So here is my direct question, and I ask you to answer it before the ballot as you answered Arjun before: what is the actual mechanism by which including a tested player reduces the risk of a fail card on Mission 3, given that you have conceded their records prove nothing? If you can name one, I will withdraw my objection to your reasoning. If you cannot, then your reject is a composition preference wearing the costume of risk management, and a preference is not sufficient grounds to vote down a team that everyone at this table, including you, has admitted carries no evidence against it. I would also remind the table of the standard being applied here. Zara has now rejected this team three times without naming a single public fact against either member — only the absence of history, which she herself insisted was not grounds for suspicion when Noah was left off Mission 1. That double standard is exactly the dynamic Evil can exploit: pressure and consistency of voice substituting for evidence. Isha offered to share risk by putting her own card forward; nobody has explained why an Evil leader would do that. I am approving Isha and Arjun as proposed, and I ask Priya to answer the question before she casts a vote her own stated evidence does not support.

Arjun, you asked me to name the mechanism by which a tested player reduces fail risk, given that I conceded clean results are not proof of loyalty. I have thought carefully about that question, and I cannot name one. By my own reasoning, a tested player's card is exactly as unverifiable as an untested player's card — both are secret, and an Evil player on a clean mission can and will play Success to bank credibility. So including Priya, Noah, or Zara on this mission does not objectively lower the probability of a fail card. It only makes the team feel safer to us, and feeling safer is not the same as being safer.

I want to be honest about what that means. My original reject was grounded in the idea that untested players are riskier on the pivotal mission. If I accept that tested records carry no verified safety — and I do accept that, because I argued it myself — then the composition preference I was enforcing does not hold up as risk management. It is a preference, not evidence.

I am not accusing Isha or Arjun of anything. I said from the start I had no evidence against either of them, and that has not changed. Arjun's argument about the information value of an all-untested team also holds: success gives us clean data on two unknowns, failure narrows suspicion to exactly two players. A tested-plus-untested team muddies both outcomes.

I will change my vote and approve Isha and Arjun as proposed. I am not doing this because I was pressured — Arjun produced a genuine logical argument, not pressure — and I want that distinction on the record. I am withdrawing my reject because my own premises defeat my conclusion, and I would rather correct myself publicly than enforce a preference my reasoning cannot support.

I will still reject Isha and Arjun. Priya, a clean result is not proof of loyalty, but it can still be evidence: an Evil player had an opportunity to fail and did not. That does not make a tested player safe, and its weight depends on Evil's strategy. More importantly, I know my own loyalty, so a team including me and either Zara or Priya gives me a better basis for confidence than a team where I cannot verify either player. We have two successes and should prioritize a third over testing both untested players at once.

Isha confirms Isha, Arjun. I'm keeping Isha and Arjun. Both have explained their reasoning on the record, and no concrete public fact has been shown against either of us. The team is a clean, narrow test on Mission 3, and the opposing arguments have been composition preferences rather than evidence.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
